en.title: Weight-Loss Pens: Losing Weight Got Easier… But What About Your Health?
en.excerpt: Weight-loss pens are everywhere — in consultations and in conversations between friends. A nutritionist on who they are really indicated for, and what they do to your health.
en.content:
Text: Nutri Marcela

Instagram: https://www.instagram.com/marcela.holisticnutrition/

A reflection on the physical, nutritional and emotional impacts of using these medications

Today I want to talk about the so-called “weight-loss pens”, a topic that is trending everywhere… on social media, in consultations and even in conversations between friends and family.

The movement is so strong that, in some cases, people even feel excluded for not using them, as if this were necessary to be part of society, often without thinking about their own health.

This ends up reinforcing a thinness standard that is often unattainable, unrealistic and, above all, unsustainable for most people.

💉 What are the “weight-loss pens”?

In fact, that is not the most accurate name. These medications were developed for the treatment of obesity and type 2 diabetes, with a medical indication and proper follow-up.

They work by mimicking a hormone naturally produced by our body, called GLP-1, which acts mainly in the intestine, helping to regulate hunger, increase satiety and improve blood glucose control.

And did you know that some of these mechanisms can also be stimulated naturally? The quality of our food, mindful eating and even the order in which we eat our food can influence satiety and our body’s response.

👩‍⚕️ Who are these medications indicated for?

These medications, known as GLP-1 analogues, are important and bring real benefits when properly indicated.

According to international guidelines, they are generally indicated for people with obesity (BMI ≥ 30) or overweight (BMI ≥ 27) associated with comorbidities, such as type 2 diabetes, insulin resistance, hypertension, high cholesterol or cardiovascular disease.

And it is important to make this clear: I am not against the use of these medications. On the contrary, they represent an important advance in health and can bring more quality of life to people who genuinely need them.

But the reflection remains: does everyone who is using them have an indication?

⚠️ Points of attention when using them

Today we live with an intense pursuit of fast results, especially when it comes to aesthetics. And, in this context, it is essential to look beyond the number on the scales.

Mental health, for example, deserves attention. Your relationship with your body, with food and with your own image can be deeply affected.

Another warning point is the use of these medications in an inadequate way, without medical follow-up, obtained inappropriately or even counterfeit. This represents a real risk to health.

🥗 The role of nutrition in this process

One of the effects of these medications is a reduction in appetite, along with possible side effects such as nausea, sickness and constipation.

But this raises an important question: how can you guarantee food with nutritional quality if you are eating much less?

Without proper guidance, your intake can become insufficient in important nutrients, such as protein, vitamins and minerals.

And that is when consequences start to appear, such as hair loss, fatigue, nutritional deficiencies and a worse quality of life.

In addition, eating less can lead to the loss of lean mass, that is, muscle loss, which directly affects metabolism and health in the long term. This process can increase the risk of sarcopenia and also contribute to a more pronounced weight regain in the future.

🧠 Hunger, behaviour and “food noise”

Many people report that, with the use of the medication, the so-called “food noise”, or eating noise, decreases.

But it is important to remember that hunger is an important physiological signal from our body. We should not be afraid of it. The goal is not to eliminate hunger, but to learn to understand it and regulate it.

And more: these medications do not directly treat emotional hunger. If there is no work on eating behaviour, these patterns tend to return when use is interrupted.

🔄 What happens afterwards?

One point that needs to be considered is what happens after the weight loss.

The body, naturally, tends to reduce metabolism as an adaptation mechanism. In other words, keeping the weight off can become a bigger challenge.

In addition, when there is a significant loss of muscle mass, the risk of weight regain increases even more.

And this leads us to an important reflection: if we are talking about medications used for chronic conditions, are we not facing treatments that may be necessary for life?

💚 A final reflection

In the pursuit of quick solutions, we often forget that health is a process.

Taking care of the body involves food, movement, mental health and behaviour.

There is nothing wrong with wanting to lose weight. But it is important to reflect: is this being done for health or only for aesthetic pressure?

Being thin is not a synonym for being healthy.

True transformation happens when we manage to build a more balanced relationship with our body and with food.

As Carl Jung said:

“What you resist, persists. What you accept, transforms.”

If you have an indication for the use of these medications, talk to your doctor and seek proper follow-up.

Now, if the motivation is only aesthetic,

it is worth reflecting with more care. Not everything that seems easy at the start is sustainable in the long term.

If you want to understand better how to take care of your food in a balanced and sustainable way, and with more awareness, I am here to help you.

Online and in-person appointments in Dublin and Kilcock

@marcela.holisticnutrition

With warmth,

Nutri Marcela 💚
en.meta_desc: A nutritionist on who weight-loss pens are really indicated for, the risks of unsupervised use and why nutrition matters.

en.title: The Pen Sheds Weight… Does the Spirit Catch Up?
en.excerpt: The weight-loss pen works fast — but is your nervous system ready? A systemic therapist on what rapid weight loss does to your emotions, your habits and your sense of identity.
en.content:
Text written by: Aria Milioni

Systemic Therapist

“It works fast… but did your heart get the warning?”

Over the last few months, I have heard the same sentence in many sessions:

“Aria, I am thinking about using the pen… they say it works really fast.”

And yes — it works. But the question almost no one asks is: what happens to the

nervous system, to the emotions and to the identity when the body changes too

fast?

I am not speaking against medicine — I speak as someone who follows closely what

happens inside people when the body changes before the mind and the heart

are ready.

Because losing weight fast is not only losing weight. It is going through a transformation that

involves the body, the nervous system and the way you see yourself in the world.

And that deserves respect — not haste.

“Less hunger on the plate… more silence in your emotions?”

Medications such as Mounjaro (tirzepatide) were created to treat type 2 diabetes.

They mimic hormones that reduce appetite, increase satiety and stabilise

glucose.

In practice, you eat less — and lose weight.

But there is something profound here: hunger is not only from the stomach. It is also from the heart.

Many people eat to relieve anxiety, compensate for sadness or fill emotional

voids. When food decreases quickly, that emotional pathway is affected too.

And the nervous system feels it.

“Your nervous system did not get the instruction manual”

When the body starts eating far less, fast, it goes into adaptation.

During use, many people report:

● intense satiety

● reduced pleasure from food

● nausea and fatigue

● mood swings

● a feeling of apathy or “switching off”

This happens because food also regulates emotions.

When that regulation changes too fast, the nervous system needs to find new

ways of balancing — and that does not always happen smoothly.

Some people become anxious. Others irritable. Others feel a silent emptiness.

It is not weakness. It is the body trying to reorganise itself.

“And when the pen leaves the scene… who holds the emotions?”

When use is interrupted, the body tries to recover its previous balance.

And that can bring:

● increased hunger

● the return of emotional appetite

● weight regain

● a feeling of losing control

But there is something even deeper: if the weight changed fast, but the emotional patterns remained, the body can return to the old behaviour — not out of failure, but out of survival.

The body tries to protect the old identity.

And that can generate shame, guilt, fear of gaining weight again — and even emotional

dependence on the medication.

I have seen people who lost many kilos… but still felt trapped inside themselves.

“New body, old inner story?”

Losing weight fast changes the body — and changes how the world looks at you.

More attention. More comments. More expectations.

And the heart is not always ready for that.

Some people feel proud. Others find their own reflection strange.

Because the body changes fast — but identity needs time.

There is also something delicate: for many people, weight works as emotional

protection.

Protection against exposure. Against vulnerability. Against old memories.

When weight drops fast, that protection can disappear — and old emotions

emerge.

And that needs to be held with care.

“Not every heart is ready to lose weight fast”

Not every emotional story can sustain fast changes.

Profiles that need more caution include:

● people with a history of binge eating

● intense anxiety or emotional instability

● a history of trauma or abuse

● a highly critical relationship with their body

● people who lose weight because of external pressure

It is not about forbidding. It is about understanding whether your system is ready.

“When the body loses weight… the soul needs to catch up”

From a therapeutic and energetic point of view, losing weight fast is a change of identity.

The mind needs to update the image it has of itself.

The heart needs to deal with new emotions.

The soul needs to integrate a new way of existing.

When that does not happen, misalignment appears.

The body changes — but inside, the feeling remains the old one.

Because weight is not only fat. It is history. It is memory. It is accumulated emotion.

If you are considering using the pen, perhaps the most important question is not:

“Will this work?”

But rather:

“Do I have support to sustain who I am going to become?”

Going through this process with therapeutic and emotional support helps to sustain:

● new forms of regulation

● new habits

● the reorganisation of identity

● the integration of the new body image

Not as something mystical — but as conscious care.

“It is not about fear… it is about awareness”

If you are using it, thinking about using it, or have already used it — it is not about guilt.

It is about awareness.

Medicine has its place. But true transformation happens when body,

mind and heart walk together.

Because losing weight is not only lowering the numbers on the scales.

It is going through a deep inner process.

And when that is done with support, presence and listening — the result is not only a

lighter body.

It is a lighter life.

And that… yes… is real transformation.
en.meta_desc: A systemic therapist on what rapid weight loss does to the nervous system, emotions and identity — and why support matters.

en.title: Physical Activity Should Not Be a Summer Project, It Should Be a Project for Life.
en.excerpt: Twelve-week challenges produce twelve-week results. A personal trainer on why the habits you can keep matter more than fast fixes.
en.content:
Text: Ana Paula, Personal Trainer

https://www.instagram.com/fitandstrongwithana/

It is very common to see “12 weeks to lose X kilos” programmes. And, along with them, come extreme solutions: exhausting workouts every day and severe food restriction. Yes, this can even produce fast weight loss… but the most important question is: could you keep that lifestyle going?

Probably not. Because it is not sustainable.

And here is a truth, based on my own experience: I lost 35 kg and have kept that result for more than 7 years. What many people do not realise is that the habits that made me lose weight are, to a great extent, the same ones that help me keep the weight off today. Of course, I make adjustments according to the phase of life, but the foundation stays the same.

There is no shortcut. There is consistency.

Another important point: physical activity should not be seen only as a tool to “burn calories”. And, above all, cardio alone is not the best strategy for weight loss.

Strength training (weight training) is fundamental in this process. It helps preserve and increase muscle mass, which improves metabolism and contributes to more lasting results. Cardio, on the other hand, has an essential role for cardiovascular health, energy and well-being, and should not be seen only as a means of losing weight.

If you want to improve something in this process, start by changing your mindset:

instead of chasing fast results, chase habits that you can sustain.

Because in the end, what brings results is not what you do for 12 weeks, it is what you can keep for life!

Movement is medicine!

To age with health, independence and quality of life, we need to stay strong.
en.meta_desc: Why 12-week weight-loss programmes fail, and how strength training and habits you can sustain beat extreme diets and endless cardio.

en.title: SCALING IS ESSENTIAL! Growing Consistently Is the Next Level for Your Business!
en.excerpt: Scaling is not just about selling more: it is about growing with strategy, structure and the right people by your side.
en.content:
By Sonia Campos, Master's in Information Science and Specialist in Business Intelligence.

instagram: https://www.instagram.com/soninhafields/

In the world of entrepreneurship, there is a clear difference between having a business and building a business that THRIVES. Many entrepreneurs start out with energy, dedication and good ideas, but few truly understand the right moment to scale and, above all, how to do it in a structured and sustainable way.

The truth is that every business has a maturation period. Just as a tree does not bear fruit the day after it is planted, companies also need time to put down roots: validating the product, understanding the audience, fine-tuning processes and consolidating their positioning. Skipping this stage can be costly. Respecting that time, on the other hand, is what prepares the ground for solid growth.

But there comes a moment when not growing becomes the biggest risk.

Scaling is not just selling more. It is growing with strategy, with predictability and with the structure to sustain that growth. And here is an essential point: nobody scales alone.

One of the biggest mistakes an entrepreneur makes is believing they have to handle everything themselves. They do not need to, and they should not. Strategic partnerships, smart hiring and the support of qualified professionals are essential to minimise risks and speed up results. Having someone who has already walked the path beside you can prevent costly mistakes and shorten the distance between where you are and where you want to be.

What is more, scaling demands clarity of goals. Wanting to grow is not enough; you need to define how, how much and in how much time. A well-structured scaling goal guides decisions, directs investment and keeps the focus on what really matters.

And speaking of growth, we cannot ignore the power of digital. PAID TRAFFIC, for example, is today one of the most effective tools for scaling a business with speed and precision. It makes it possible to reach the right audience, at the right moment, with a strategic message. But it is not the only path.

Other ways of scaling include:

* Building authority through content;

* Strategic positioning on social media;

* Process automation;

* Well-structured sales funnels;

* Partnerships and collaborations with other professionals and brands.

Each of these strategies, when well applied, helps to turn effort into scalable results.

Throughout my journey as an entrepreneur, Digital Marketing teacher, mentor and influencer, I have learned that growing is not about doing more — it is about doing better, with direction and intelligence. I love technology, I believe in the power of education, and my mission is to teach other entrepreneurs to see beyond operations and move to a more strategic level in their businesses.

If there is one thing I can say with conviction, it is this: growth is part of the process, but it has to be built.

Respect your business's timetable, but do not settle into it. Seek strategy, surround yourself with the right people and have the courage to take the next step.

Because in entrepreneurship, growing is not luck. It is a decision.
en.meta_desc: Why scaling demands strategy, structure and support, and how to grow your small business consistently without losing direction.

en.title: 🌿 Spring Has Arrived: An Invitation to Renew Your Nutrition Too
en.excerpt: Spring changes more than the landscape — it is also the perfect moment to bring more colour, freshness and nourishment to your plate.
en.content:
Text: Nutri Marcela

Instagram: https://www.instagram.com/marcela.holisticnutrition/

Spring has arrived, and with it the days grow longer… The daffodils (those beautiful yellow flowers) begin to appear everywhere, and a new energy of renewal, after winter, starts to emerge here in Ireland.

And along with that energy, this is also a great moment to look at our food with more care. To think about how spring can be a great ally for lighter, more nutritious and more balanced eating.

When we talk about healthy eating, following the seasons makes all the difference. Seasonal foods also matter a great deal in this process. So when you find products such as Irish carrots or Irish spinach, choose those options, because they tend to be fresher, tastier and better for our planet too.

And today I want to show you how, with small steps, we can make the most of this season to make our food tastier and more nutritious — not only for you, but for your whole family.

 

💚 A little about me

I am Marcela Ferreira, a nutritionist. I have lived in Ireland for 14 years and I work with a gentle nutrition approach, grounded in science and free of extremes.

My focus is to help you build a way of eating for life, improve your relationship with food and make more conscious choices — whether your goal is to lose weight, look after your health or improve a test result.

Because, more than numbers, how you feel matters. And caring for your diet is not only about what we do today, but about what we can keep up over the years, creating a healthy and sustainable eating pattern.

And that is why thinking about how to eat well in each season is also part of this process.

For example, in winter… who really feels like eating salad? Our body naturally asks for warmer, more comforting meals.

But that is a subject for another conversation. Today let us focus on spring 🌸 and on how we can make our food lighter, more nutritious and more in tune with this new season.

 

 

🌸 How to adjust your eating for spring in practice

Spring here in Ireland still arrives with milder temperatures. It is only around May that we begin to feel a little warmth — or rather, to put away the heavier coats.

We also do not yet have a great variety of local fruit and vegetables at this stage, and that is absolutely fine.

The most important thing here is not perfection, but a simple principle: the more colours on your plate, the better.

If you do not usually include vegetables in your meals yet, start little by little. Try adding at least one vegetable to lunch and dinner.

And an important point: frozen vegetables are excellent allies too. They are just as nutritious as fresh ones. The same goes for frozen fruit.

If you do not like them much, start by choosing the ones you already enjoy. The idea is to gradually bring more colour and variety into your everyday life.

Remember: progress is better than perfection 💚

 

🥗 Do not forget the pulses

Another important point is to include more pulses in your diet.

Our traditional rice and beans, so present in our culture, is an incredible example of nourishing, comforting food, and it can, and should, remain part of your routine.

Here in Ireland, you will find a wide variety of beans in supermarkets such as Tesco and Dunnes, as well as in the Brazilian shops.

An important tip is to soak the beans for at least twelve hours and change the water at least once. When cooking, use fresh water and, if you like, add a few drops of vinegar or some bay leaves.

This process helps improve digestion, reduce gas and even makes the beans more nutritious.

And pay attention to the extras. Processed meats such as bacon and sausage should be eaten more occasionally, and not every day.

You can also vary things with other options such as chickpeas, lentils and even hummus. Even the ready-made one from the supermarket can be a good option, or you can make your own version at home.

A practical snack idea is hummus with carrot. Simple, nutritious, and many children take to it very well.

And yes, tinned pulses can be an option too. Give preference to versions with no added salt or preserved in water. Just remember to rinse them well before eating, as this helps reduce excess sodium and can also lessen the digestive discomfort, such as gas, that some people report.

Variety is essential for our health, and it does not have to be perfect every day. Think across the whole week.

 

🐟 Include fish in a simple way

Another point that is well worth it in Ireland is making the most of the easy access to fish, such as salmon.

A simple way to prepare it is to season with salt and olive oil and bake at two hundred degrees for about twenty minutes.

You can serve it with potato, carrot and broccoli. Everything can be prepared practically, even in the same pot, with the potato and carrot in water and the broccoli steamed.

 

🫒 And do not forget the olive oil

Olive oil is a great ally for your health and it is very affordable here.

Prefer to buy it in a dark glass bottle and store it in the cupboard, away from the light.

 

💧 Hydration counts too

And a simple but essential reminder: drink water.

Hydration helps your bowel function, your energy, your mood and your body's balance.

Finally, here is an invitation for you to reflect, with this renewing energy of spring. What can you improve in your diet today, even in small steps?

Remember: progress is always better than perfection.

If you feel you need help to organise your eating, look after your health through nutrition, improve your relationship with food or bring more balance to your daily routine, I am here to help you.

Online and in-person appointments in Dublin and Kilcock

Instagram: https://www.instagram.com/marcela.holisticnutrition/

With love,

Nutri Marcela 💚
en.meta_desc: A gentle nutritionist's guide to eating with spring in Ireland: seasonal food, pulses, fish, olive oil and simple everyday steps.

en.title: Spring: The Silent Call to Bloom with Awareness
en.excerpt: Spring does not ask us to rush into results. It invites us to bloom through awareness, patience and the quiet work of tending what we choose to live.
en.content:
Text: Juliana Gomes

Founder of the Escola Mulher Sistêmica

Instagram: https://www.instagram.com/juliana.mendes.gomes/

The arrival of spring in the northern hemisphere is not just a change of season. It is a subtle yet profound invitation to move through a state of transition — one of those that are not always visible on the outside, but that stir our inner world intensely.

After the withdrawal of winter, life begins to rise again. The light returns, the days expand, nature awakens. And, along with it, something in us moves too. Spring calls us to bloom, to begin new cycles, to open what was previously gestating.

But blooming is not just about beginning.

Blooming requires presence, support and maturity.

There is a time between the initial impulse and the concrete manifestation of what we wish to live. A time we often neglect, because we were taught to seek quick results, immediate answers and paths without a crossing.

Spring teaches us the opposite.

It reminds us that everything that is born needs care. That what begins needs to be nourished. That the beauty of blooming lies not only in the result, but in the silent process of growth that happens day after day.

For us women, this understanding is even more essential. Because life invites us not only to do, but to gestate. To respect our rhythms, our inner timing, our capacity to sustain what we choose to live.

And perhaps the greatest challenge of this time is precisely this: not to lose yourself in the many possibilities that arise, but to remain connected to what truly matters.

Spring is fertile.

But not everything needs to bloom.

Discerning, choosing and sustaining are movements of feminine maturity.

Returning to awareness of the cycles is returning to our place.

It is learning to walk with more truth, less haste and more presence.

Spring has arrived.

And with it, the opportunity to bloom — not by impulse, but by awareness.

At the Escola Mulher Sistêmica, we look at life from this perspective: that we are part of a greater cycle, and that when we disconnect from it, we also lose our own direction.

Our School is here, close to you, in County Laois, as a living space of reconnection, maturity and belonging to the cycle of life.
en.meta_desc: Spring as a call to grow with awareness: why blooming asks for presence, patience and maturity — not speed or immediate results.

en.title: Moist Coconut Cake (Cocada Molhadinho)
en.excerpt: A budget-friendly coconut cake that bakes up soft and creamy inside, finished with a sweet coconut and condensed-milk drizzle.
en.content:
Chef Sonia Campos @grannymadeireland

​

Ingredients:

3 eggs

A few drops of vanilla (optional)

1 tin of condensed milk (395g)A pinch of salt

150g desiccated or flaked coconut

1 small bottle of coconut milk (200ml)

1 cup (120g) cornflour

1 tablespoon (16g) baking powder

​

Method:

Preheat the oven to 180°C and grease a medium tin with butter and cornflour or flour.

In a blender, add the eggs, the condensed milk, the coconut milk, the vanilla (if using) and the pinch of salt. Blend for about 2 minutes until smooth.

Add the desiccated coconut and the cornflour. Blend again until well combined.

Add the baking powder last and stir gently with a spoon, or blend briefly just to combine.

Pour the batter into the prepared tin. Bake for about 35 to 45 minutes, or until nicely golden on top.Let it cool a little before cutting. It stays slightly creamy inside — that is the perfect texture of this moist coconut cake!

Tip from Chef Sonia Campos: To make it even moister and tastier, mix:3 tablespoons of coconut milk1 tablespoon of condensed milk.

Drizzle this over the cake while it is still warm and finish with desiccated coconut on top.

It is simply irresistible!
en.meta_desc: Chef Sonia Campos' moist coconut cake: a simple blender recipe with a coconut and condensed-milk drizzle to finish.

en.title: FINANCIAL MANAGEMENT: the invisible foundation of every business that thrives
en.excerpt: Working hard and selling well is not enough if you cannot see where the money goes. These six foundations keep a small business healthy.
en.content:
By Sonia Campos, Master's in Information Science and Specialist in Business Intelligence.

instagram: https://www.instagram.com/soninhafields/

Many small entrepreneurs work hard and sell well, yet at the end of the month they still feel that there is never any money left.In most cases, the problem is not a lack of sales, but a lack of financial organisation.

Looking after the company's finances is not just about controlling spending. It is about understanding where the money goes, how it comes in and how it can grow. Below are the essential points for every beginner entrepreneur:

​

1. Keep the company's finances separate from your own.

Mixing personal money with company money is the most common and the most expensive mistake. When that happens:

  • Real profit becomes hard to identify

  • Cash flow gets muddled

Important decisions end up based on gut feeling, not on numbers

The solution: open a separate bank account for the company and pay yourself a fixed salary. That guarantees clarity and security.

​

2. The right price is essential

It is not enough to charge “what the customer is willing to pay”. The price needs to cover:

Fixed costs (rent, bills, equipment)

Variable costs (raw materials, packaging, commissions)

Taxes

Adequate profit margin

Without this, you may well be selling a lot, but losing money without realising it.

​

3. Profit is a tool, not a prize

When there is profit left over, many spend it all. Solid companies use profit to:

  • Improve processes

  • Invest in marketing

  • Buy better materials

  • Build a financial reserve

Businesses that reinvest grow; businesses that consume everything stagnate.

​

4. Have a financial reserve

Problems happen. A financial reserve prevents panic when cash flow tightens. It helps you to:

  • Get through weaker months

  • Avoid emergency debt

  • Make decisions without pressure

You do not have to start big, but start now, even little by little.

​

5. Always keep track of the numbers

You do not need complex systems, but daily control is essential. Be clear about:

  • How much came in

  • How much went out

  • Future obligations

  • Where losses are occurring

Those who do not track the numbers work in the dark. Those who do, decide with confidence.

​

6. The biggest risk is losing money without noticing

Many entrepreneurs make sales but see no profit because:

  • They price incorrectly

  • They spend without control

  • They do not track the numbers

If you feel that there is never any money left, the problem is not how much you sell, but how you manage what comes in.

 

Conclusion:

Financial management is not bureaucracy, it is strategy. Entrepreneurs who understand their numbers:

  • Make better decisions

  • Reduce losses

  • Create consistent growth

If you feel that you work hard and money never seems to be left over, sound an EMERGENCY alarm: perhaps you are working for the sake of working, letting slip the profit opportunities that could make your business take off.

Sonia Campos Business Intelligence SpecialistConsultant and University LecturerMaster in Information Science

en.title: When the Earth Awakens: Spring and the New Astrological Year
en.excerpt: Spring arrives as a quiet turn of energy, and with the Sun in Aries it opens a new astrological year of movement, direction and gentle courage.
en.content:
Text written by: Aria Milioni

Systemic Therapist

There is a moment in the year when energy changes direction — quietly, almost

imperceptibly. It is like when the body wakes before the alarm clock and something inside you

starts to flow again.

Spring begins like this.

After the withdrawal of winter, life pushes outwards again. The light increases, the air

changes, and a natural desire arises to reorganise, move the body and decide what was previously

on hold.

Astrologically, this portal coincides with the entry of the Sun into Aries — the beginning of the

New Astrological Year.

If January opens the social calendar, March opens the calendar of the soul.

Aries represents the first impulse of life — the seed that breaks through the earth. It does not ask for

perfection, it asks for movement. That is why, at this stage, many people feel more energy,

positive restlessness and the need to begin something new.

After the dive of Pisces, which cleaned and closed cycles, the question arises:

“And now, what are you going to do with who you have become?”

Spring is not only about flowers — it is about direction.

In mental health, this is an important period for choosing where to place your energy. The

mind wants to act, but alignment comes from awareness, not from excess. Ask yourself: what

really deserves my attention now?

Emotionally, the season asks for a gentle courage — allowing yourself to take up more space and

to seek relationships more coherent with who you are today.

In the physical body, the energy of Aries needs movement so that it does not turn into tension. Walking

more, stretching, returning to physical activity and receiving natural light help the nervous system to leave

winter mode.

In practical life, this is the ideal moment to start projects, reorganise routines and test

new directions without demanding immediate results. It is a phase of conscious

experimentation.

Aligning yourself with the New Astrological Year is not about changing everything at once, but acting from

a truer place.

If winter asked “what needs to end?” spring asks “what deserves

to be born?”

Choosing a living intention — something that can be felt in the body — is already enough to

open the way.

The New Astrological Year is an organic new beginning. A whisper from nature saying:

“Now you can move forward.”

The invitation is to move, without losing the inner listening that winter taught — so that action

and awareness walk together, and this new cycle is lived with presence, direction and

vitality.

Aria Milioni

Text written by: Aria Milioni

Systemic Therapist

en.title: Between the Silence of Winter and the First Breath of Spring
en.excerpt: February is a quiet corridor between what has ended and what is still being born — a month of inner honesty rather than maximum productivity.
en.content:
(February as a portal of transition)

Text written by: Aria Milioni

Systemic Therapist

There is a moment in the year when life seems to breathe more slowly.

It is not the height of winter, when everything is already clearly withdrawn.

Nor is it spring yet, with its open promise of movement and expansion.

February is that sensitive interval — a silent corridor between what has ended and what

is still being born.

Energetically, it is a month that stirs deep layers.

Old emotions can reappear, tiredness becomes more visible, and a strange mixture

of impatience and apathy emerges. As if one part wanted to move forward… while

another still needs to rest.

Astrologically, February usually moves through Aquarius and Pisces — archetypes of

liberation and dissolution.

Aquarius opens windows. It questions patterns, breaks old mental structures and shows what

no longer fits the version of us that is emerging.

Pisces, soon after, softens our defences. It brings sensitivity and reveals where there is still pain

not yet felt, grief not yet processed, dreams forgotten.

That is why February can be emotionally intense even when, outwardly, nothing

“big” happens. Inside, a great deal is reorganising itself.

This is not a month of maximum productivity. It is a month of inner honesty.

In the mind, it invites us to review narratives:

— Which thoughts no longer make sense for the person I am today?

— Which decisions do I keep postponing for fear of changing?

In the emotions, the invitation is to feel without haste — not to resolve everything, but to allow

old processes to complete themselves.

In the physical body, the request is simple and therapeutic: more rest than performance, more

warmth than demands, deep breathing, gentle stretching, slow walks.

The nervous system is still in winter mode.

And winter is not a mistake of nature — it is the laboratory where roots grow.

In the practical areas of life, February is a month of adjustment, not of expansion.

It is when we realise what truly deserves energy when spring arrives — what

continues, what ends, what needs a new form.

Spring does not arrive suddenly. It begins as a whisper: a day with more light,

a deeper breath, a new idea that appears effortlessly.

To navigate February wisely is not to force flowers before their time.

It is to allow:

● closing cycles without drama

● resting without guilt

● reviewing priorities honestly

● releasing habits that no longer sustain the next version of yourself

● caring for the body as fertile soil

If winter was the time to withdraw, February is the time to listen to what inside you

wants to be born.

And when spring finally opens — within and without — what was tended in silence

turns into natural movement, not effort.

Perhaps the true invitation of this month is not to do more, but to slow down enough to

notice who you are becoming.

Because it is in that space between the end and the beginning that life decides, with tenderness, what

your next form will be.

Aria Milioni

Text written by: Aria Milioni

Systemic Therapist
en.meta_desc: February as a portal between winter and spring: why it can feel so intense, and how to move through it with rest, honesty and gentleness.

en.title: Purpose: The Meaning That Moves Us From Within
en.excerpt: Purpose is not a prize waiting to be found — it is an inner compass we hear with the heart and allow to come alive through what we give.
en.content:
Text: Juliana Gomes

Founder of the Escola Mulher Sistêmica

Instagram: https://www.instagram.com/juliana.mendes.gomes/

I received with joy the invitation from dear Tati to write for this magazine for Brazilian women and men in Portlaoise. It is an honour to be able to share reflections on a theme as essential as it is delicate: the purpose of life.

My name is Juliana, I am Brazilian, I am 43 years old and I have lived in Ireland for nine years. I am the mother of Lia, the wife of Thiago and the founder of the Escola Mulher Sistêmica, a school of feminine consciousness based on the Natural Laws of Cooperation of Life, laws that reconnect us to the natural cycle of existence, to ancestry and to the deep sense of belonging.

And it is precisely about meaning that I want to talk with you today.

The word “purpose” is one of the most repeated of our era. Many of us look for quick answers: What is my purpose? How do I find it?

But perhaps the truest question is another:

What if purpose is not something you find, but something that reveals itself when there is space?

Purpose is not just a mental concept. It is an intimate, spiritual and emotional perception. We women especially, so burdened by external demands, often try to understand life only with our heads, when purpose can only be heard with the heart.

In my experience, purpose is not to be confused with who we are, nor is it limited to what we do professionally. Purpose is that which moves us from within. It is a sense of direction, like an inner compass pointing to where the soul wishes to walk.

When we are aligned with that sense, life gains more harmony. But, in the crossings of being human, we often lose our way. And this happens because we live disconnected from our essence and from the natural cycle of life.

I like to think of purpose as we think of our children: we conceive them, care for them, educate them, but they do not belong to us. One day, they take on the world. Purpose is like that too. It does not stay tied to us. It needs to come alive. It is an offering.

A great part of the emotional illness of our era is born precisely from this disconnection: burnout, anxiety, chronic stress. It is not only an excess of tasks, it is the absence of meaning in what you give.

Reconnection, however, can begin simply. A few minutes of silence. A conscious breath. A prayer. Intimate writing. A sincere request to return to your essence.

Because it is not only what we do, but how we do it.

Sometimes, it will be necessary to recalculate the route. In some cases, purpose lies within the current path, but with a truer “how”. In others, it will be necessary to listen to an old call that has long been waiting for courage.

And it is important to remember: purpose is not a prize for those who search, but a process for those who surrender.

May this text be just a small opening. An invitation for you to breathe and ask yourself:

What in me wants to come alive now?

Which meaning wants to move me?

Gratitude

Juliana

Founder of the Escola Mulher Sistêmica
en.meta_desc: A reflection on purpose as an inner compass: why meaning is felt rather than found, and what reconnecting with it asks of us.

en.title: Aligning the Invisible to Harmonise Daily Life
en.excerpt: Chakras and crystals, ancestral symbolism and energetic sensitivity: an invitation to pause and reconnect with yourself.
en.content:
Text: Janine Meira Henriques

Holistic Therapist, writer, playwright, artist, photographer, journalist, mother of 4 children.

Training: Degree – journalism, performing arts, holistic therapies, courses  including reiki, radionics, Access Bars, astrology and tarot. Psychology degree in progress, completion due in June 2026.  

Postgraduate studies: Brazilian literature, human sexuality.

 

In recent years, integrative practices that bring together spirituality and personal care have been gaining ground in conversations about quality of life. Among them, work with chakras and crystals stands out for combining ancestral symbolism, energetic sensitivity and an invitation to self-knowledge.

 

The chakras, subtle energy centres distributed throughout the body, are traditionally associated with different physical, emotional and spiritual aspects of the human being. When these centres are in balance, the vital flow tends to circulate more freely, favouring a feeling of lightness, mental clarity and emotional stability. When blockages are present, feelings of anxiety, excessive tiredness or difficulty in expressing emotions may arise.

 

It is in this context that crystals come in as natural allies. Each stone has a vibration of its own, formed over thousands of years by pressure and by the elements of the earth. When placed close to the body or used during moments of meditation, they can act as energetic catalysts, helping to release tensions and restore the harmony of the chakras.

 

For example, rose quartz is often associated with the heart chakra, stimulating compassion, empathy and self-love. Amethyst, linked to the frontal chakra, is seen as a support for intuition and mental serenity. Citrine, related to the solar plexus, inspires confidence and vitality.

 

More than a technique, aligning the chakras with crystals can be understood as a ritual of pause and presence. By dedicating a few minutes of the day to breathing, feeling and observing, a person creates an inner space of listening, reconnecting with themselves and with their deepest needs.

 

In a fast-paced world, where doing often outweighs feeling, this practice invites us to slow down and remember that balance is also born of silence, of attention and of respect for our own energy. After all, caring for the chakras is, in essence, caring for the life that pulses inside each one of us.

en.title: Building a Support Network Far From Home
en.excerpt: Far from home, expatriate mothers can rebuild the support network they miss — here are practical, accessible ways to start in Ireland.
en.content:
Written by: Lili Fraga – Family & Children Intercultural & Emotional Development

Connections that strengthen immigrant wellbeing

Living outside your country of origin is, in itself, a dive into the unknown. But for expatriate mothers, the challenges multiply. Motherhood away from home carries layers of longing, tiredness, fear and, often, the temporary loss of your own identity. Who you were before you left seems distant — and now, as well as a mother, you are also an immigrant, starting from scratch in a place where you do not always speak the language or understand the social dynamics.

The absence of your support network — that grandmother, that friend, that neighbour — is sorely felt. The routine becomes heavier, rest becomes rarer, and self-esteem can begin to weaken. The good news? Even far from home, it is possible to build new networks. Perhaps different from the ones you knew, but just as powerful, genuine and welcoming.

Help does not always appear spontaneously, and that is okay. But know this: you can find or create spaces of support that hold you emotionally, help with the challenges of everyday life and remind you that you are not alone.

💡 Practical strategies for finding your network in Ireland

Here are some real, accessible ways to step out of isolation and start connecting with other people who share similar values:

👩‍👧‍👦 1. Groups for mothers and fathers (Parent & Toddler Groups)

Community spaces where mothers (or fathers) and their small children gather to play, socialise and swap experiences. Many are free or cost a token amount. 🔎 Where to find them: Family Resource Centres, local churches, crèches or community centres. E.g.: A Mother’s Embrace (Waterford), Barnardos, TUSLA parent support groups.

🤱 2. Bilingual or cultural playgroups

Taking part in groups that respect and celebrate your culture (such as groups of Brazilian or Latin American mothers) helps you feel seen and welcomed. 🔎 Look for groups on WhatsApp, Facebook (“Brasileiras na Irlanda”, “Mães em Dublin”, etc.), or in community schools.

☕ 3. Cafés for immigrants and themed in-person meet-ups

Moments designed to create connections: conversation circles, workshops, wellbeing and motherhood events. 🔎 Follow local projects such as Mum talks https://www.instagram.com/mum_talks/ 

🧘 4. Activities that combine self-care and company

Yoga classes, walking groups, art workshops or guided meditation with other mothers. A lovely way of looking after yourself while socialising. 🔎 Search Eventbrite, Meetup or Instagram for local activities using keywords such as “mothers”, “community wellness”, “creative circles”.

A few apps that can help you find the right group for you: – meetup.com– peanut-app.io– letsmush.com– nextdoor.ie

📱 5. Create your own network!

If you have not found anything that fits you, create it! A coffee at home with other mothers, a virtual support group and a picnic in the park. Someone is always waiting for that invitation.

💛 Wrapping up…

Connections heal. Belonging strengthens. Being seen transforms. Even far from your homeland, you can — little by little — rebuild your support network, surround yourself with people who welcome who you are today, and experience motherhood with more lightness and truth.

📌 And remember: seeking support is not selfishness. It is wisdom. You deserve to be well in order to care — including for yourself.

en.title: How Do You Feel at This Time of Year?
en.excerpt: Short days, grey skies and constant cold affect your mood and energy. Recognising seasonal affective disorder is the first step to caring for yourself.
en.content:
Lili Fraga –

Therapist and Parent Educator

Have you ever stopped to think about how your body and your emotions react to the arrival of autumn and winter here in Ireland?

Of course there are people who enjoy the chill, the silence, being cosy in their own little corner — and that is perfectly fine if that is you. But for many of us, especially those who came from tropical countries or from places with well-defined seasons, this time of year can be challenging.

The short days, the grey sky and the constant cold affect our mood, our energy and even our self-esteem. This has a name: scientifically, we call it Seasonal Affective Disorder (SAD) — a type of depression related to the change of season, common in countries of the northern hemisphere (GUZMAN et al., 2007; SAHEER et al., 2013).

In addition, studies with immigrants show that the feeling of isolation and low exposure to natural light intensify symptoms such as sadness, fatigue, irritability and lower immunity (SAHEER et al., 2013).

That is why, now more than ever, this is a time to observe your own behaviour with tenderness and compassion. Recognising what affects you is the first step towards turning discomfort into care.

🌱 What if we met up?

Know that you have a real opportunity to meet other people, laugh, talk and feel part of something bigger. The group of Brazilians in Portlaoise is turning 5 years old — and, to celebrate this beautiful journey of mutual support and connection, there will be a special in-person meet-up in the park. (Event postponed, a new date will be announced).

Contact with nature and with other people is a powerful way of looking after your mental health, especially at this time of year.

Studies prove that frequent exposure to green spaces is directly associated with reduced anxiety and depression, as well as promoting the release of hormones related to wellbeing (TANG et al., 2023). Another survey reveals that 20 to 30 minutes in natural environments are already enough to reduce cortisol levels and increase the feeling of social connection (WHO, 2021; GASCON et al., 2015).

Being outdoors, with people who share the same journey, is an invitation to welcome, affection and belonging.

💡 Practical tips for looking after yourself in winter:

✅ Make the most of natural light, even if only for a few minutes a day.

✅ Move your body — walks, dancing or stretching already help a great deal.

✅ Eat with intention — bananas, nuts, oats and cocoa stimulate serotonin.

✅ Talk to someone — join groups, call a friend, seek therapy.

✅ Plan small weekly pleasures — a coffee, a book, a hot bath.

✅ And if you can: come to the in-person meet-up! Being with other people warms the heart.

✨ Do not let winter freeze you from the inside. Let us keep going together, creating human warmth, looking after our mental health and celebrating every step of this journey away from home — but ever closer to ourselves.

📍See you at the park? It will be beautiful to share this moment with you.

With affection, Lili Fraga – Therapist and Parent Educator http://www.instagram.com/lilifraga.vivaleve
en.meta_desc: How autumn and winter in Ireland affect your mood and energy, and practical ways to care for your mental health through the darker months.

en.title: 2. Mental Health and Immigration: What Nobody Tells You
en.excerpt: What almost nobody tells you about moving abroad: the anxiety, loneliness and pressure that arrive along with the suitcases — and where to find help in Ireland.
en.content:
Text: Lili Fraga –

Therapist and Parent Educator

Central theme: Anxiety, loneliness and depression among immigrants

Talking about the emotional impact of starting over in another country, the pressure to succeed, and how to find help (in Portuguese or English) in Ireland. Including warning signs and paths to support.

🧠 Mental Health and Immigration: What Nobody Tells You

Anxiety, loneliness and depression far from home

Have you ever heard that phrase “Just come!” when someone talks about living abroad, doing a study exchange or moving to another country? Well… it sounds like a light invitation, full of promises — freedom, opportunities, money, quality of life. But what almost nobody tells you is that, along with the suitcases, come the doubts, the pressures, the longing and, often, the emotional silence.

Sometimes the desire to change is so intense that we set off without looking deeply into our inner possibilities. We lack the time (or the courage) to ask ourselves: “Am I ready for this fresh start?” Because yes, living abroad is a transformative experience — but it demands an immense emotional maturity.

Worries are not limited to housing or work. They invade your sleep, your mood, your vital energy. Starting over, reinventing yourself and, above all, finding yourself are key pieces so that you do not lose yourself along the way.

Living abroad demands emotional planning and deep listening:

●      What are my limits?

●      How do I deal with frustrations?

●      Am I willing to live the new without cancelling who I am?

And this is where the central point of this conversation comes in: mental health in immigration.

🔍 The psychological impact of starting over

Studies indicate that immigrants show higher rates of anxiety, depression and post-traumatic stress than local populations. This happens for several reasons: social isolation, language difficulties, culture shock, financial insecurity and lack of a support network (FERREIRA, Alisson Vinícius Silva; BORGES, Lucienne Martins, 2022; WHO, 2018).

In Ireland, a study with Brazilians revealed that many live with significant levels of stress, especially women and mothers who feel overwhelmed because they are the pillar of the family while facing cultural and language barriers (Ribeiro et al., 2020).

⚠️ Warning signs

Noticing that something is wrong is not always easy. But pay attention to a few signs:

●      Difficulty sleeping or waking up rested

●      Constant irritability or crying spells with no apparent reason

●      Lack of motivation, loss of pleasure in simple things

●      Self-deprecating thoughts or a feeling of inadequacy

●      A feeling of loneliness even when surrounded by people

●      Intense anxiety in the face of ordinary tasks (going to the shop, talking to someone, leaving the house)

These symptoms are not weakness. They are requests for help.

🧭 Paths to support

If you recognised yourself in any of these situations, know that you are not alone — and you do not have to face this without support. Here in Ireland there are resources available, both in Portuguese and in English:

🌿 Support in Portuguese:

💛 Wrapping up…

Dealing with mental health in immigration is an act of courage. It means stepping out of denial and saying: “I matter. My feelings are valid. And I deserve support.”

You do not have to be fine all the time. But you can aim to be fine with yourself, even on difficult days.

en.title: 1. Caring for Yourself in a Foreign Land
en.excerpt: Emotional difficulties, overwhelm and longing for family are part of starting over abroad — but simple self-care practices can protect your mental health.
en.content:
Text: Lili Fraga

Therapist and Parent Educator

Central theme: Self-care as a tool for adapting to immigration

Emotional difficulties, overwhelm, missing your family and the feeling of always being in survival mode. How can you create moments of pause, connection with yourself and simple practices to protect your mental health even with little time or resources?

✨ Caring for Yourself in a Foreign Land

A look at the emotional wellbeing of those starting over outside Brazil

Living far from your country of origin can be challenging. Beyond the demands of everyday life, the immigrant faces deep emotional layers — often marked by the feeling of not belonging. Some discover themselves to be incredibly resilient and recognise their inner strength. Others decide to return to their country. And there are those who take on the challenge of seeking a new place in the world. What we do know is that we Brazilians — with our warm blood, our easy laugh and our open affection — carry far more than other people's eyes can see.

The truth is that there is no single path to happiness and wellbeing. Feeling well far from home invites us on a journey of self-discovery, where we learn to respect our limits, to accept that we will not always be understood and that we may not manage to please everyone. Sometimes we need to create our own space in order to feel at ease within discomfort.

And this is not just poetry. Studies show that self-care practices (such as creating routines, maintaining social bonds or spirituality) are fundamental to the mental health of immigrants and refugees, with psychological and social strategies being the most effective in preventing anxiety, sadness and chronic low mood (Mehjabeen et al., 2023). In addition, public health researchers in Ireland highlight the importance of having access to culturally sensitive services that respect our language, our history and our pace of adaptation (McMahon et al., 2021).

Looking after our wellbeing is necessary. Building relationships that allow us to be who we truly are is crucial to walking this path of starting over, where emotional bridges may look fragile but can be built with affection and courage.

And that is why I invite you to look at one moment at a time, to make your choices based on your own reality and to live at peace with yourself. You will see that happiness really can be part of this nomadic life of yours — not as a fixed destination, but as a state of presence.

If you need help, do not hesitate to ask for it. Far from home, we can build a new home — as long as we are aware of the pillars that hold it up.

🗓️ Next month, we will talk about: “Mental Health and Immigration – What Nobody Tells You”. We will make room to talk about anxiety, insomnia, guilt, and what to do when it feels as though we are losing our strength.

See you there. With affection, Lili Fraga – Therapist and Parent Educator http://www.instagram.com/lilifraga.vivaleve
en.meta_desc: A therapist's guide to self-care while adapting to life abroad — and why culturally sensitive support matters for immigrants in Ireland.

en.title: Courage! The Star That Lights the Entrepreneur's Path — Christmas Special
en.excerpt: Christmas lights remind us of the flame we so often let go out: courage. A short reflection for entrepreneurs closing the year.
en.content:
The end of the year always invites us to pause for reflection.

Christmas lights illuminate not only the streets of our cities, but also something we so often let go out along the entrepreneurial journey: the flame of courage.

Being an entrepreneur is, above all, an act of faith. Faith in an idea, faith in a purpose, faith in your own ability to get up after every stumble. Because stumbles will come, and they are not a sign of weakness.

​

They are part of the route. In fact, nobody builds anything extraordinary by walking in a straight line. Great business stories are born exactly in the detours, in the course corrections, in the ability to stop, take a deep breath and decide to try again.And here is a truth few will tell you. Money is not enough.

An academic background is not enough. It is not enough to have taken every course, been through mentoring, studied diligently. These elements help a great deal, but they do not sustain a business on their own. The backbone of entrepreneurship, yesterday, today and always, is courage! Courage to start.Courage to take calculated risks and uncalculated ones.Courage to recalculate the route a thousand times, if need be.

Courage to carry on, even when nobody else understands what you see.While some believe that entrepreneurship is about strategy, others think it is about capital. But we know: entrepreneurship is about heart. About putting your soul into every attempt and understanding that growth is not a destination, it is a continuous movement.

This Christmas, allow yourself to celebrate not only the results, but above all the journey. Celebrate the attempts, the falls, the fresh starts. Celebrate every time you dared to believe, even when everything seemed uncertain.

And may the coming year bring new routes, new ideas, new possibilities and the courage needed to follow them.Happy Christmas!

May this season renew your strength, your faith and your determination to keep creating, daring and building.
en.meta_desc: A Christmas reflection for entrepreneurs on why courage, not money or qualifications, keeps a business moving forward.

en.title: Two New Years: One Measured by Man, Another Felt by the Earth
en.excerpt: The Gregorian calendar organises society, while the solar return — when the Sun enters Aries — governs vitality. Learning to honour both changes the rhythm of the year.
en.content:
Text written by: Aria Milioni

Systemic Therapist

Once upon a time — not in the sky, but on paper — human beings decided where the year should begin.

The Gregorian calendar was created to organise society, not consciousness; dated 1582, it was introduced by Pope Gregory. It aligns contracts, taxes, harvests, work, debts and systems of governance. Time became something that could be counted,

regulated, audited and controlled. The reason was this: for civilisation to work on a large scale, a common agreement was needed — and so 1 January was chosen as the starting line: clean, numerical, administrative.

This calendar governs the material agreement of life: bills to pay, deadlines, fiscal years, the school calendar, productivity targets. It belongs to the constructed dimension of reality, where continuity, control and predictability are essential. It does not answer to nature — it organises people.

And that is not a flaw. It is its function. And nothing beyond that.

But alongside this created rhythm, there is another year — one that does not begin by decision, but by alignment.

The solar return, in energetic and astrological terms, happens when the Sun enters Aries. That moment marks the true beginning of the solar cycle. It is when light begins to overcome darkness, when the Earth tilts once more towards growth, when life receives the signal to move forward. This is not symbolic; it is seasonal, biological, energetic.

Aries inaugurates movement. The seeds awaken. The blood warms. The systems spring into action. Long before calendars existed, life on Earth was already responding to this change. That is why many ancient cultures recognised spring — and not the middle of winter — as the true New Year.

The solar return governs energy, not administration.

It rules vitality, instinct, initiative, courage and birth.

It belongs to nature, to astrology, to time lived in the body.

So we live inside two simultaneous cycles, two dimensions of existence, two

timelines.

One begins in January and asks:

How will you manage your life?

How will you pay, plan, organise, maintain?

The other begins when the Sun enters Aries and asks:

How will you live it?

What wants to be born, to be initiated, to be embodied?

Winter — January, February and much of March in the northern hemisphere — exists between these two thresholds. By the Gregorian calendar, it looks like a beginning. By the solar calendar, it is still a closing.

That is why so many people feel discomfort in early January.

The system says “move forward”.

The body answers “not yet”.

Winter is the last chapter of the energetic year. It is the phase of fertile decomposition. The nervous system slows down. The psyche reviews. The body conserves. Expecting full performance during this period is not discipline — it is misalignment.

Caring for yourself while respecting both systems is learning to speak two languages.

● Mind: Use January to organise, not to launch. Plan without demanding immediate execution. Structure without pressure.

● Body: Honour low energy as functional, not as failure. Sleep more. Eat more densely. Move gently.

● Emotions: Allow introspection. Winter brings truths to the surface so that they do not sabotage spring. Emotions are information, not obstacles.

Then, when the Sun enters Aries, something changes naturally. Action stops being forced.

Decisions gain warmth. Direction becomes clear.

The Gregorian calendar keeps society running.

The solar return keeps you alive.

When both are honoured, life stops feeling like resistance — and becomes rhythm.
en.meta_desc: Why early January feels wrong: the Gregorian calendar says advance while the body says not yet, and Aries is the real solar new year.

en.title: Movement Is Medicine!
en.excerpt: A personal trainer on staying strong after 30, building routines clients can truly keep, and why exercise is a commitment for life.
en.content:
Text: Ana Paula, Personal Trainer

https://www.instagram.com/fitandstrongwithana/

As a woman over 30, I understand how difficult it is to fit a training routine into everyday life. However, I also know how essential it is, because from that age onwards we start to lose muscle mass more quickly, which has a direct impact on bone density. Weight training is the best tool to fight that process, and that is why I insist so much on building routines that my clients can genuinely keep in the long term — for life.

As a Personal Trainer, my mission is to help each client find the best exercise routine, aligned with their reality and their lifestyle, so that training is continuous and sustainable — and not something momentary. After all, physical exercise is a commitment for your whole life, not only a way to achieve the “summer body”.

My name is Ana Paula, I am a Personal Trainer with 5 years of experience in the field. I am passionate about movement and about helping, especially beginners, to take the first step into an exercise routine, also promoting a better relationship with exercise and food.

Over these five years of work, I have also taken vocational courses in the areas of Nutrition and Mat Pilates, because I believe that constant upskilling is essential. To really contribute to improving physical health, which is directly linked to mental health, it is essential to keep updating yourself and, above all, to listen to each client, respecting their history and their experiences.

Movement is medicine!

To age with health, independence and quality of life, we need to stay strong.
en.meta_desc: Why strength training after 30 protects muscle and bone — and how to build an exercise routine you can genuinely keep for life.

en.title: Getting the Body Ready for Winter
en.excerpt: Autumn asks us to slow down: warming root vegetables, good fats and rest, to build immunity before the quiet of winter.
en.content:
The role of food, rest and rootedness in the transition of autumn.

Text: Simone Holz

Holistic Nutritional Therapist

Autumn is the season when mornings begin to turn colder, the sun says goodbye earlier and nature quietly changes its rhythm. The trees release what no longer serves them, and that same movement invites us to introspection, to turn inwards, nourish the roots and prepare body, mind and soul for the stillness of the

winter that is approaching.

Just as the earth reorganises itself, our body also enters this process of adaptation. It is common, in the first weeks of autumn, to feel the body heavier, muscles and joints more sensitive, a tiredness that arrives without warning or a deeper sleep that asks for more time to rest. All of this is natural: the

organism is detoxifying the excess of heat, sugar and stimulation from summer, the ice creams, the long days, the fast pace.

Autumn is nature’s gentle reminder that it is time to slow down, clear what has accumulated and strengthen our foundations. It is the time to “ground the roots” and let

go of what has already played its part, whether toxins, emotions or habits that no longer sustain our vitality.

During autumn, our body starts asking for more nutritious, denser and warmer food, and not without reason. It is the moment when we need to strengthen our

immune system and create energy reserves for winter.

This is the phase of nourishing and fortifying. Nature already offers us exactly what we need: food from the earth,

such as root vegetables – potato, carrot, beetroot, turnip, parsnip. Which are naturally richer in complex carbohydrates and minerals, providing stable energy and sustaining inner warmth. It is as if the earth itself were saying: “the time to put down roots has come.”

In Irish culture, this ancestral wisdom is reflected in the stews, coddle and soups typical of that season, warm and comforting dishes that combine root vegetables,

pulses and herbs, a simple and delicious way to warm the body and strengthen immunity.

Besides that, this is the moment to look with care at the nutrients that sustain our natural defences. Vitamin C, present in citrus fruits, kiwi and peppers,

helps protect the cells; zinc, found in pumpkin seeds and nuts, is essential for immune function; and selenium, present in eggs and

Brazil nuts, has a fundamental role in regulating thyroid hormones and in antioxidant protection. Vitamin D, often reduced by less

sun exposure, can be strengthened through foods such as oily fish (salmon, sardines) and eggs, or with professional guidance for supplementation. Small adjustments in the diet make a big difference in the body’s ability to face the cold with balance and vitality.

Another essential point is caring for the gut microbiota, the foundation of our immune system. Including fermented foods, such as sauerkraut, kefir, kombucha or natural yoghurt, helps keep the gut healthy and the body more resistant to infections. Good fats such as olive oil, avocado, seeds and nuts nourish the cells, support hormonal balance and favour the production of serotonin and melatonin, neurotransmitters linked to mood and sleep, which tend to fluctuate at this time of year. This dietary transition, at once simple and wise, stabilises blood sugar, calms the nervous system and prepares the body for the withdrawal of winter with strength and serenity.

Autumn is an invitation to pause, a space between doing and being, between the movement of summer and the withdrawal of winter. It is the moment to quieten the external noise a little and listen to the body, which wisely shows what it needs: more rest, more warmth, more presence. Preparing for winter is not only about strengthening

immunity, but about cultivating an inner state of balance and being held.

Every nutritious meal, every well-slept night, every conscious breath is an act of love and respect for the body that sustains you. When you allow yourself to slow down and nourish your roots now, you create fertile ground to go through the cold months with energy, clarity and serenity.

This autumn, listen to your body. Slow down, warm your soul and trust the natural process of the seasons.

By aligning yourself with the cycle of nature, you discover that winter is not the end, it is the rest necessary for the blossoming that will come.

Simone Holz

Holistic Nutritional Therapist
en.meta_desc: How to prepare the body for winter: seasonal root vegetables, fermented foods, vitamin C, zinc, selenium and vitamin D, plus rest.

en.title: The Warmth That Is Born of Winter
en.excerpt: Winter slows the world down — and asks us to choose what we want to see grow. A reflection on inner warmth, rest and creativity.
en.content:
Text: Ana Luiza A Duarte

Integrative Therapist

Winter arrives with its dense air, its short days and a certain inevitable withdrawal. And, while the world seems to fall asleep, something in us begins to wake. It is the time to listen to what the body asks for, what the heart whispers, what the soul wants to preserve.

Cold is, at times, a form of care: it slows us down, preserves and protects what is still to bloom. And, since it is a time to conserve and prepare, perhaps winter is also an invitation to choose.

Before sowing the seeds, you need to know what you want to see grow. Which dreams deserve to germinate when the sun warms the earth again? Which ideas, affections or plans do you

want to nourish now, in the silence, so that they sprout strongly when the season changes?

Because inner warmth is not limited to the body — it can take the form of ideas that ignite, of intentions that warm up, of plans that take shape even under the cold.

They are small embers that keep alive the hope of a new flowering.

While outside everything seems still, inside us something reorganises itself. What looks like a pause is, in truth, preparation. Rest is the fertile ground of everything that is to come.

There is a kind of warmth that does not come from fire — it is born slowly, in silence, when the cold invites us to turn inward.

It is a warmth that springs from the heart and needs to be tended with care. The mind, when fed by prosperous thoughts, by ideas that inspire and by gestures that awaken creativity, helps to keep that flame alight. This warmth heals us, wakes us and allows us to give new ideas their first flight — small sparks that can bring us closer to ourselves and to the people around us.

Perhaps it is precisely this withdrawal that allows us to access our creative source.

To create, we need to become sensitive to what surrounds us, to perceive the possibilities around us, to choose what inspires us and to transform it into something unique — an action, an expression, an idea that carries passion and determination. When the noise outside diminishes, we can hear those subtle voices within us, the ones asking for space, form and colour.

Winter, with its calm, creates the perfect ground to imagine and recreate what we want to live.

So light your small campfires: a book, a song, a hot soup, a good memory. Allow yourself that warmth that is born from within and spreads slowly.

Winter is a reminder that true warmth is not only in the sun — it is in what we choose to nurture when the world grows cold.

Ana Luiza A Duarte

Integrative Therapist
en.meta_desc: Winter as a time to rest, choose what to nurture and light the inner warmth that keeps creativity and hope alive until spring.
